skills.name: Soil: components and an open system

note.text: Soil is a living, developing surface material containing mineral particles, organic matter, organisms and pores holding water or air. It supports plants and stores and transmits water and nutrients. Weathering contributes mineral material; decomposing remains contribute organic matter. Soil is an open system: rainfall and litter enter, while drainage, gases, harvest and erosion can remove material. The proportions vary with soil, depth and conditions. More pore water usually leaves less pore air at a fixed pore volume; saturation can restrict oxygen available to roots.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to identify soil components and balance air and water within a stated pore-space model. Builds on: Form Three’s weathering and land-surface processes. Leads to: soil properties, profiles and erosion.

sections.heading: Follow the local example or model
sections.text: In an invented Buea garden comparison, rain enters pore spaces that previously held air. This changes moisture and aeration without turning mineral grains into water. The calculation uses a classroom mixture totalling {100}%, not a prescription for every real soil. A soil organism is living; humus is relatively decomposed organic material rather than another name for all mineral grains.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Identify solids, organisms and pore contents separately. When shares are given for a whole, subtract every stated share once. Explain an input or output by tracing what crosses the chosen system boundary. Do not taste soil or handle unknown contaminated samples; the screen model supplies all data needed.

example: Weathering supplies sand, silt and clay to a garden soil.

cards.idea: Explain how the process produces the stated effect.
example: Mineral particles differ from organic residues even when mixed together.
Organic matter originates from organisms and differs from mineral rock.
A water-filled pore remains a pore; its contents have changed.
Inputs, outputs and internal transfers make soil a changing open system.
